newsitem.title: USA: Electric vehicle U.S. road rally gears up.
newsitem.headline: Electric vehicle U.S. road rally gears up.

text.p: Fancy and far out electric cars of all sizes will jostle for position in the American Tour de Sol, the Indianapolis 500 of electric and solar-powered vehicles, organisers said on Friday.

The week-long trek will pit 50 "alternative energy" vehicles against each other in a 350-mile (563 km) rally through the back roads of New England, including a climb up Mount Washington in New Hampshire.
The cars will not race, but will be competing for three prizes, with the emphasis on showing that electricity-powered vehicles can be practical alternatives to gasoline-power.
"It's a practical demonstration of the viability of alternative-energy vehicles," said Jim Whitney, executive director of the Waterbury Convention and Visitors' Bureau.
During the rally the entries will travel at normal highway speeds and in normal traffic conditions. No roads will be blocked off.
"It's under normal traffic conditions. That's the point of the whole thing," Whitney said.
Prizes will be awared for greatest distance travelled without recharging, for miles per equivalent gallon of gasoline and for consumer acceptability.
The ninth annual rally begins on May 19 in Waterbury, Connecticut, and winds up on May 23 in Portland, Maine.
This year's event features entries from major manufacturers Ford Motor Co. and Toyota Motor Corp..
Spurred partly by anti-pollution measures passed in California, many auto makers have switched their electric vehicle programmes into high gear, analysts said.

General Motors and Honda Motor Co. Ltd. have electric vehicles available for lease in California, said Nancy Hazard, associate director of the Massachusetts-based Northeast Sustainable Energy Association (NESEA).
Other big manufacturers, including Chrysler Corp., Toyota, Nissan Motor Co. Ltd., and Mazda Motor, are expected to have electric vehicles on the market in 1998.

"It's switched from a hobbyist thing to a business. The vehicles have gotten much better," said Charles King, director of electric transportation at Northeast Utilities, which is participating in Ford's electric vehicle demonstration programme.

King said price and range are still the main barriers to broad acceptance of electric cars. Many of the vehicles get only 60-75 miles per battery charge, and the Ford and General Motors Corp. models will have suggested list prices of more than $30,000.
"That's the price of a new technology," he said. "But for uses like commuting or delivering things around the city, it's an ideal little vehicle," he said of the Ford Ecostar.
Massachusetts-based Solectria has already sold about 200 vehicles, Hazard said.
"The industry isn't going to turn around overnight," she said. "We're talking decades before we see a large portion of the vehicles being electric."

"But we really believe that (switching) to electric vehicles is really good for the economy in addition to the environment. There is the potential for a tremendous reduction in oil imports and oil usage in the U.S."
